web-accessibility-sr1-02.statement: WCAG guidelines provide the pass-or-fail checks used to decide conformance.

web-accessibility-sr1-10.statement: Publishing WCAG 2.2 left WCAG 2.1 and 2.0 in place as current W3C Recommendations.
web-accessibility-sr1-10.explanation: WCAG 2.2 does not deprecate or supersede WCAG 2.0 or 2.1, so content can still conform to those earlier versions as current Recommendations.

web-accessibility-sr2-12.reason: ambiguous: 'authors still assess 4.1.1' describes practice, and WCAG 2.2 itself says authors bound to 2.0/2.1 'may need to continue to test and report 4.1.1'. Rewritten as a true statement of what WCAG 2.2 contains, plus the reason the Understanding page gives ('Assistive technology used to do their own parsing of markup, but now rely on the browser'). Turning it true moves r2 from 4/6 to 5/5 after the two drops, and removes one of the always-false 'level as predicate' cards. Removal is tested once in the deck. (final: keep)
web-accessibility-sr2-12.statement: In WCAG 2.2, 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed because assistive technology now relies on browsers to parse HTML.
web-accessibility-sr2-12.explanation: Assistive technology used to parse markup itself. Many issues that once failed Parsing now fail Info and Relationships or Name, Role, Value instead.

web-accessibility-sr3-09.reason: weak_card (strawman: bold CSS creating th semantics), rewritten because dropping all four flagged r3 cards would leave 8. The verifier's replacement was confirmed on MDN main: 'A document mustn't have more than one <main> element that doesn't have the hidden attribute specified.' It adds coverage of the main landmark. factKey: single-visible-main-element. (final: keep)
web-accessibility-sr3-09.statement: HTML allows two visible `<main>` elements on one page when each has a unique accessible label.
web-accessibility-sr3-09.explanation: A document may have only one main element without the hidden attribute, so a label cannot make a second visible main valid.
web-accessibility-sr3-09.misconception: A unique accessible label lets a page repeat the main landmark the way it can repeat nav or region landmarks.

web-accessibility-sr4-05.reason: source_problem: MDN aria-label never states replace-versus-append. The APG says: 'If aria-label is applied to an element with one of the roles that supports naming from child content, content contained in the element and its descendants is hidden from assistive technology users.' Statement and answer kept; explanation takes the verifier's sourced wording. (final: fixed)
web-accessibility-sr4-05.statement: On a button, `aria-label` appends its text to the name supplied by the button's content.
web-accessibility-sr4-05.explanation: If aria-label is set on a button, its value replaces the name the button would get from its content; the content is hidden from assistive technology users rather than appended.
web-accessibility-sr4-05.misconception: aria-label supplements rather than replaces the button's content-derived name.

web-accessibility-sr5-05.explanation: aria-valuenow is role-specific: WAI-ARIA 1.2 uses it on range roles such as slider, spinbutton and scrollbar, while aria-label and aria-describedby are global.

web-accessibility-sr6-04.statement: In WAI-ARIA 1.2, `aria-pressed="mixed"` marks a toggle button whose controlled items hold differing values.
web-accessibility-sr6-04.explanation: aria-pressed is tri-state: true, false or mixed. Mixed means the items the button controls do not all share the same value; the default, undefined, means the element is not a toggle.
